searchDocs.title: Standard Install
searchDocs.content: Standard Install Unity Catalog Required SAT requires Unity Catalog. Make sure Unity Catalog is enabled in your Databricks environment before installing SAT — the app stores its results (and its credentials, as UC secrets) in a Unity Catalog schema. What the standard install does ./install.sh runs locally (Python 3.9+), asks for your CLI profile and a SQL warehouse, and deploys the security-analysis app to your workspace. Everything else — catalog/schema, account credentials, scope, and compute — is configured in the app's setup flow after it is deployed. App source folder The installer uploads the app code to /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool. If you deploy or redeploy the app from the Databricks Apps UI (Compute → Apps → security-analysis → Deploy), choose that folder as the app's source code path. From the CLI it's databricks apps deploy security-analysis --source-code-path /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool. SAT can be set up on any of the cloud platforms where Databricks is hosted. Please follow the setup guide specific to your cloud provider: AWS Setup GuideAzure Setup GuideGCP Setup Guide Note We welcome your feedback and comments — please reach out to us at sat@databricks.com or open a GitHub issue. Please review the Project Support section for important information on support and usage terms.

searchDocs.title: How the app is organized​
searchDocs.content: Home — a landing overview of your account's scope (workspaces, account groups and admins) and quick entry points into the analyses below.Principal Analysis — start from a user, group, or service principal and see everything it can reach, with admin roles (Account / Workspace / Metastore Admin, Catalog Owner) and the workspaces/metastores each admin administers.Resource Analysis — start from a resource (catalog, schema, table, cluster, job, warehouse, secret scope, notebook, or folder) and see every principal that can reach it, and whether access is direct or inherited through a group.Credential Exposure (secret scanning) — hardcoded secrets found in notebook source, workspace files, and cluster configurations, with scan settings and custom detection rules. See Secret Scanning.Alerts — email/notification alerts on secret-scan findings, built on Databricks SQL alerts. Creating and editing alerts is restricted to workspace or account admins.Security Assistant — a chat assistant (backed by a Databricks Foundation Model and a Genie space) that answers questions about your findings and permissions, enforcing your own Unity Catalog grants on every answer.Data Collection — run and schedule the collection jobs on demand, and manage scan scope, compute, and notebook/folder collection (see theManage panel).Settings — change the results catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, model, or account credentials at any time.

searchDocs.title: Who sees what​
searchDocs.content: The app runs queries as the signed-in user (on-behalf-of), so Unity Catalog enforces each viewer's own grants on the results — people see only the data they are entitled to. Administrative actions are gated accordingly: creating, editing, and deleting alerts requires the signed-in user to be a workspace or account admin.  Access to the app itself Grant "Can Use" on the Databricks App only to the people who should operate SAT. App access is the boundary for running collection jobs; viewing results is further constrained per-user by Unity Catalog. We strongly recommend limiting app access to administrators — ideally having admins be the sole users of SAT. Keeping the operator set small and admin-only keeps this security data on a need-to-know basis. Non-admins who only need to read findings should be granted Unity Catalog read access to the results schema instead of "Can Use" on the app.

searchDocs.title: Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before you begin, ensure you have:  ✅ Reviewed the general prerequisites✅ Appropriate permissions in your Databricks Account Console✅ A metastore attached to your installation workspace✅ Databricks CLI installed and configured✅ Python 3.9 or higher (3.9–3.12, for running the local installer)

searchDocs.title: Step 1: Create Service Principal​
searchDocs.content: The Service Principal allows SAT to authenticate with your Databricks workspaces and collect security information.  How to create a Service Principal Follow these steps in the Databricks Account Console: Navigate to the Account ConsoleClick on User management in the left sidebarSelect Service Principal → Add service principalEnter a name for the service principal (e.g., "SAT-Service-Principal")Grant the Account Admin roleAssign the Workspace Admin role for each workspace to be monitoredAdd to the Metastore Admin group or roleCreate a new OAuth SecretSave the Secret and Client ID (you'll need these later)Add the Service Principal to each workspace you want to analyze Required Permissions: Account Admin roleWorkspace Admin role for each workspaceMetastore admin group membership

searchDocs.title: Step 2: Run Installation​
searchDocs.content: Credentials Required Have these ready for the app's in-app setup (you enter them in the app after install, not during install.sh): 🔑 Databricks Account ID🔑 Databricks Service Principal ID (Client ID from Step 1)🔑 Databricks Service Principal Secret (from Step 1)

searchDocs.title: Installation Steps​
searchDocs.content: Run these commands on your workstation or a VM with internet access and Databricks workspace connectivity:  1. Clone the SAT repository:  git clone https://github.com/databricks-industry-solutions/security-analysis-tool.git cd security-analysis-tool   Databricks CLI Required Make sure the target workspace has a profile configured in the Databricks CLI.  2. Make the installation script executable and run it:  chmod +x install.sh ./install.sh   Proxy Support Proxies are supported! You can add your HTTP and HTTPS proxy values during the install.sh script when prompted.  3. Follow the interactive prompts:  The installation script will guide you through the setup process. Here's what it looks like:      Finish setup in the app After install.sh deploys the app, open it (Compute → Apps → security-analysis) and complete the in-app setup — results catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, and (optionally) account credentials for account-wide data. Permissions Analysis is built into the app; there is no separate app to configure.  Deploying the app — choose the source folder install.sh uploads the app code to /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool and deploys it for you. If you ever deploy or redeploy from the Databricks Apps UI (Compute → Apps → security-analysis → Deploy), you must select that folder as the app's source code path. From the CLI the equivalent is databricks apps deploy security-analysis --source-code-path /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool.  Scanning multiple workspaces To cover more than the workspace SAT is installed in, add the SAT service principal as a workspace admin on each workspace you want scanned, then in the app open Data Collection → Manage, set Compute & scope to Multiple workspaces (switching to Multiple runs a workspace sync for you), and confirm the panel's "Will scan: N workspaces" count. Use Manage → Sync workspaces any time you later add or remove the service principal as an admin. See the usage guide for the full workflow.  Congratulations! 🎉 You've successfully installed SAT on AWS Databricks.  Installation Complete SAT is now ready to analyze your Databricks workspaces. Click here for a detailed guide on how to run and use it.

searchDocs.title: After installing​
searchDocs.content: The Terraform install deploys the SAT app and binds its SQL warehouse (the sqluser-authorization scope is declared automatically — no manual UI step). Finish in the app:

searchDocs.title: 1. Complete the in-app setup​
searchDocs.content: Open Compute → Apps → security-analysis → Open and complete setup — results catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, and (optionally) account credentials for account-wide data, plus scope and compute. See the Usage Guide.

searchDocs.title: 2. Grant Unity Catalog access for per-user reads​
searchDocs.content: The app runs queries as the signed-in user (on-behalf-of), so Unity Catalog enforces each caller's grants on the Permissions Analysis tables. Grant SELECTon those tables to the users or group who will run permissions analyses:  GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_vertices TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_edges TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_collection_metadata TO `<admin_group>`;   Tip Replace <catalog>, <schema>, and <admin_group> with the values used during your SAT install. More on user authorization and the friendly no-access banner is on the Permissions Analysis page.

searchDocs.title: Why Use SAT?​
searchDocs.content: Databricks has worked with thousands of customers to securely deploy its platform, leveraging security features that meet diverse architectural requirements. While security implementations vary across organizations, there are commonly adopted guidelines and features used by organizations with high security standards.  SAT helps you:  🔍 See Who Can Access What Build a complete graph of users, groups, and service principals and the resources each can reach — directly or inherited through groups. 🧭 Spot Risky Access Surface privilege-escalation paths to admin roles and impersonation / lateral-movement risk via jobs and clusters. 🔑 Find Exposed Secrets Detect hardcoded credentials in notebook source and cluster configurations, with your own custom detection rules. 📋 Audit-Ready Reports Over-privileged users, orphaned resources, high-risk principals, and resources shared to all account users.

searchDocs.title: What SAT Analyzes​
searchDocs.content: SAT focuses on access and secret exposure:  👥 Identities & Access - Users, groups, and service principals; admin roles (Account / Workspace / Metastore Admin, Catalog Owner); and the full access graph, including access inherited through groups.🗄️ Resource Access - Who can reach catalogs, schemas, tables, clusters, jobs, warehouses, secret scopes, notebooks, and folders.🧭 Escalation & Impersonation - Paths from any principal to admin roles, and lateral movement via jobs or clusters that run as elevated service principals.🔑 Exposed Secrets - Hardcoded credentials in notebook source and cluster configurations.  Best-practice checks retired Earlier versions of SAT also ran core security posture checks (severity-ranked findings across Network Security, Data Protection, Governance, and so on) and rendered them in dashboards. Those checks are now available natively in the Databricks platform — the Governance Hub Security tab — so they and the dashboards are retired from SAT; 1.0 focuses on the capabilities Governance Hub doesn't cover: access/permissions risk and secret exposure. (If Governance Hub isn't available in your environment, e.g. AWS GovCloud, use SAT v0.9.1 for the checks.)

searchDocs.title: Important Considerations​
searchDocs.content: Assessment Tool SAT is a productivity tool that helps you understand access risk and find exposed secrets across your Databricks account. It is not intended to serve as a certification or formal attestation of your deployment's security posture.

searchDocs.title: SAT Deployment and Support​
searchDocs.content: Is SAT an officially supported tool? The Security Assessment Tool (SAT) is not officially supported by Databricks. It is provided as-is under the Databricks License, with no guarantees or Service Level Agreements (SLAs). Please do not open support tickets for issues related to SAT. Instead, report any problems or feature requests by creating a GitHub Issue on the project's repository. Issues will be reviewed as time permits. All third-party libraries referenced are subject to their respective licenses.  Can I open Databricks support tickets if I encounter issues with SAT? Currently, SAT is a self-service tool which is developed and maintained by the Databricks field team. If you encounter any issues, please contact your Databricks account team and submit a GitHub issue on the project's repository.  Can SAT be configured on an independent virtual machine? SAT needs to be deployed in one of your Databricks workspaces and run as a workflow. You can trigger the SAT installation process from any machine (preferably Linux) where the Databricks CLI and other prerequisites are available, installed and configured.  Does SAT automatically update once I set up? SAT is frequently updated and the latest versions are made available in the official GitHub repository. SAT deployments do not automatically update on their own. To upgrade or update SAT deployments in your environment, you will need to perform the update manually. This design decision is by choice, so that customers have full control on the upgrade process of SAT.  Can SAT make modifications to my workspaces and account? SAT is read-only by default — it analyzes and reports, and does not change your workspace or account configurations. The only changes it can make are ones you explicitly opt into: creating SQL alerts, and the opt-in remediation in a few account reports (for example removing an over-broad "shared to all account users" grant or an unexpected admin role), which run only when you turn them on.  I am seeing errors when I run the SAT. How can I validate my SAT configuration? Use the app's built-in requirements check: open Settings → Re-run setup and review the requirements checklist, which verifies the account connection and the service principal's Account admin role live and flags configuration gaps. For a failed collection job, open the Data Collection page and inspect that job's last run. See Troubleshooting.  How do I rotate or update the service principal's credentials (client ID / secret)? Do it from the app — no redeploy or re-provision: In the account console, create a new OAuth secret for the service principal.In SAT, open Settings → Account credentials.Paste the client ID and the new secret, then click Update credentials. They're verified before being stored (as Unity Catalog secrets), so a bad value is caught here rather than in a job log later.Once the next run succeeds, revoke the old secret in the account console. The collection jobs read the secret at run time, so the next run picks up the new value automatically — you don't redeploy the app or re-provision the jobs. The same flow lets you switch to a different service principal entirely (enter its client ID + secret); make sure that SP holds the Account admin role, and for multi-workspace scanning that it's a workspace admin on each workspace.  If SAT is already configured, how do we add/remove other workspaces in the same account/subscription? Scan coverage is driven by whether the SAT service principal is a workspace admin of each workspace. To include a workspace, add the service principal as a workspace admin on it; to exclude one, remove it. Then open Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces in the app — Sync discovers the account's workspaces and enables the ones the service principal administers (analysis_enabled in the account_workspaces table). No manual SQL, no re-running a heavy collection job. Make sure collection scope is Multiple workspaces for the scanners to cover more than the current workspace.  A workspace was deleted after SAT was set up — how do I stop it from erroring? A workspace that can no longer be reached fails its connection test on the next scan and is skipped and recorded, not failed — no reinstall needed. To drop it from the registry entirely, run Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces (Sync only keeps RUNNING account workspaces the service principal administers).  I added a new workspace — how do I get it included? Add the app's service principal as a workspace admin on the new workspace, then run Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces so SAT discovers it and enables it for scanning. Set collection scope to Multiple workspaces so the scanners cover it. No re-setup, no initializer re-run, and no dashboard pulldown or cache to refresh. (Removing the service principal as admin and syncing again drops the workspace.)  Can I use one deployment of SAT to monitor all my workspaces across different clouds, like AWS and Azure? A single SAT app monitors all workspaces in the same Databricks account — on AWS, Azure, or GCP. (On Azure this is per Databricks account, not per subscription.) A different Databricks account — for example a separate AWS account and Azure account — needs its own SAT app.  Do I need different SAT deployment to monitor workspaces in different regions? A single SAT app monitors all workspaces in the same Databricks account regardless of region, on any cloud.  Can SAT be integrated with other cloud based monitoring tools? SAT is designed specifically for Databricks. Its results live as Delta tables in your chosen Unity Catalog schema, so you can query or export them with any tool that reads Unity Catalog (DBSQL, BI tools, pipelines) and feed them into other systems as needed.  Is SAT supported on AWS GovCloud? Yes. SAT supports AWS GovCloud (FedRAMP) and AWS DoD IL5 — it resolves the correct account-console host for each (accounts.cloud.databricks.us for GovCloud, accounts-dod.cloud.databricks.mil for DoD) — in addition to commercial AWS, Azure, and GCP.

searchDocs.title: SAT Reports​
searchDocs.content: Do we need to address every finding SAT reports? Review SAT's findings with your business stakeholders, administrators, security team, and auditors, and assess them against your organizational security requirements — not every finding requires action, and some remediations have cost or dependency implications. Always review the associated feature documentation before making changes.

searchDocs.title: Core Features​
searchDocs.content: The SAT App The single app interface — permissions analysis, secret scanning, alerts, and the security assistant, all in one place. Permissions Analysis Graph-based analysis that reveals who can access what resources, plus escalation and impersonation risk, across your Databricks account. Secret Scanning Secret detection across notebook source and cluster configurations using TruffleHog, with in-app scan settings and custom detection rules.

searchDocs.title: How SAT Works​
searchDocs.content: The app provisions its own collection jobs and runs them on a schedule (you can also run them on demand):  Data Collection The collection jobs query Databricks account and workspace APIs to build a graph of your identities, resources, and permission relationships, and scan notebook source and cluster configurations for exposed secrets. Historical Tracking Results persist in Delta tables in your chosen Unity Catalog schema, for historical tracking and trend analysis. In-app Reporting You explore everything in the app — as the signed-in user, so Unity Catalog enforces your own grants on what you can see. No separate dashboard to publish or share.

searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: The SAT App - How the app is organizedInstallation Guides - Deploy the SAT app using the standard installer or TerraformUsage Guide - Complete in-app setup, run collection, view results, and configure alerts

searchDocs.title: What Permissions Analysis does​
searchDocs.content: Permissions Analysis transforms the Databricks permissions into a queryable graph database, enabling you to:  Query Access Patterns: Find all resources a user/group/service principal can access—including indirect access via group membership and parent resource inheritanceReverse Lookup Security: Discover all principals (users, groups, service principals) that have access to a specific resourceDetect Escalation Paths: Identify privilege escalation risks by finding paths from any principal to admin roles (Account Admin, Metastore Admin, Workspace Admin, Catalog Owner)Analyze Impersonation Risk: Discover lateral movement opportunities where users can modify jobs or clusters that run as elevated service principalsGenerate Compliance Reports: Produce audit-ready reports showing over-privileged users, orphaned resources, and high-risk principals

searchDocs.title: Common Use Cases​
searchDocs.content: Access Audit - Identify all principals with access to a specific resource Challenge: Manual verification takes 45+ minutes and may miss nested group memberships. Solution: Permissions Analysis provides instant reverse lookup showing all principals with access to a specific resource, including indirect access paths through group memberships and inheritance.  Privilege Escalation Assessment - Determine if a principal can reach admin roles Challenge: Manual verification requires traversing dozens of relationships to identify potential escalation paths. Solution: Permissions Analysis maps the entire attack surface, identifying all paths from any principal to admin roles (Account Admin, Metastore Admin, Workspace Admin, Catalog Owner), not just the obvious paths.  Blast Radius Assessment - Assess impact if a service principal is compromised Challenge: Determining accessible resources and running jobs requires extensive investigation before revoking credentials. Solution: Permissions Analysis queries the graph to show all resources accessible by a principal, including tables, models, clusters, warehouses, and jobs that run under the compromised identity.  Orphaned Resource Identification - Find resources without clear ownership Challenge: Identifying current responsibility for resources created by departed users is complex, especially when resources still run in production. Solution: Permissions Analysis generates compliance reports identifying orphaned resources and their current access patterns, helping determine who has implicit admin rights through ownership.

searchDocs.title: Step 1: Run Data Collection​
searchDocs.content: The SAT app provisions a "SAT Permissions Analysis - Data Collection" job and runs it on a schedule.To run it on demand:  Open the app and go to the Data Collection pageRun "SAT Permissions Analysis - Data Collection"Allow 10-30 minutes for completion (varies by account size)  The collection job queries Databricks APIs to build a complete graph of your environment's identities, resources, and permission relationships.

searchDocs.title: Step 2: What the collection builds​
searchDocs.content: Data collection and the account reports are produced by the /notebooks/brickhound/notebooks, which the app runs as jobs — you don't open or run them by hand. They populate the graph and brickhound_* tables that the app reads. For reference, here's what each produces:  Notebook (collection engine)	Purpose	Example question answered01_principal_resource_analysis.py	Query access patterns	"What tables can john.doe@company.com access?" "Who can access XYZ resource" 02_escalation_paths.py	Find privilege escalation paths	"Can this contractor reach Account Admin?" 03_impersonation_analysis.py	Analyze impersonation risks	"Who can run jobs as elevated service principals?" 04_advanced_reports.py	Generate compliance reports	"List all users with access to 50+ resources" 05_share_to_account.py	Detect & optionally remediate resources shared to all account users	"Which dashboards/Genie Agents/Apps were shared with everyone?" 06_privileged_non_idp_identities.py	Detect & optionally remediate privileged identities that are not IdP-managed	"Which non-IdP groups / direct users hold Account Admin?" 07_denylist_candidates.py	Rank account groups by inactive members for the access denylist	"Which IdP groups' members aren't using Databricks?"  note 05–07 are audit-log / account-SCIM based rather than graph based, so they do not require the data collection job to have run first. Each writes its own brickhound_* table and has a scheduled job: 05_share_to_account.py → brickhound_shared_to_account. Report-only by default; set remediate=yes to remove the "account users" ACL entry (the SAT service principal must be a member of each affected workspace).06_privileged_non_idp_identities.py → brickhound_privileged_non_idp. Flags non-IdP (no externalId) groups with Account/Workspace Admin, and users/service principals with those roles assigned directly. Opt-in remediation removes the account_admin role via SCIM.07_denylist_candidates.py → brickhound_denylist_candidates. Ranks IdP-managed (external) account groups by inactive-member count (inactive = no system.access.audit activity in the look-back window — a heuristic for the Automatic Identity Management "Inactive: No usage" status). Feeds the Account Denylist Builder tab. AIM caveat: under Automatic Identity Management, external group memberships are resolved just-in-time and are not returned by the account SCIM Groups API, so member-based ranking can be empty even for populated groups; in that case use the Entra ID dynamic-group rule builder in the app tab instead.

searchDocs.title: Step 3: Explore in the app​
searchDocs.content: Permissions Analysis is built into the SAT app — no separate app to deploy.  Open it at: https://<workspace-url>/apps/security-analysis (or Compute → Apps → security-analysis), then use the Principal Analysis and Resource Analysis pages.  The app provides:  Interactive search for principals and resourcesEscalation paths visualizationImpersonation analysis reportsAccount Denylist Builder (inactive-user group candidates + an Entra ID dynamic-group rule builder)Security reports including: Secret scope accessHigh privilege principalsOver-privileged usersOrphaned resourcesResources shared to all account users (read-only view of the latest detection run)Privileged non-IdP-managed identities (read-only view of the latest detection run)    User Authorization​  The app is intended for workspace and account admins. So that the app cannot act as a privileged proxy beyond each caller's Unity Catalog grants, the SAT install configures user authorization on the app declaratively (via DABS or Terraform) — the sql scope required by the Statement Execution API is set automatically. No manual UI step is required.  When user authorization is configured, the app constructs a per-requestWorkspaceClient bound to the caller's forwarded OAuth token and Unity Catalog enforces the caller's grants on the Permissions Analysis tables.  Required Unity Catalog grants (admin-only). Grant the users or group who will run permissions analyses SELECT on the three Permissions Analysis tables in the SAT analysis schema, e.g.:  GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_vertices TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_edges TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_collection_metadata TO `<admin_group>`;   Without these grants, opening the app shows a friendly banner naming the missing tables instead of a generic error.  Manual override. If you need to add or remove scopes manually, open the app in the Databricks UI (Compute → Apps → security-analysis → Edit → User authorization) and edit the scope list. The IaC default of ["sql"] is sufficient for normal use. SP fallback. If user authorization ever gets cleared (no scopes configured), the app automatically falls back to its service principal identity and a one-time warning is logged. Functionality is unchanged. Re-add the sql scope to restore per-user enforcement.  Re-consent after an upgrade​  If you upgrade an install where the app previously ran without user authorization, each user who had already opened the app re-consents once — they see the friendly "missing the sql scope" banner until they do. The quickest fix is to open the app URL in a private/incognito window (fresh session, the platform prompts for consent immediately); clearing cookies for the workspace domain or revoking the prior authorization from the user's connected-apps list work too. Fresh installs declare user_api_scopes: ["sql"] from the start, so a first open prompts for the right scope automatically.

searchDocs.title: Query Access Patterns​
searchDocs.content: Find all resources accessible by a specific principal, including:  Direct permissionsGroup memberships (including nested groups)Inherited permissions from parent resourcesService principal impersonation  Example Query: Determine what resources the principal john.doe@company.com can access.

searchDocs.title: Reverse Lookup Security​
searchDocs.content: Discover all principals with access to a specific resource:  Users with direct accessGroups with access (and their members)Service principals with accessInherited access paths  Example Query: Identify all principals that can access the production.finance.revenue table.

searchDocs.title: Detect Escalation Paths​
searchDocs.content: Identify privilege escalation risks by finding paths to:  Account AdminMetastore AdminWorkspace AdminCatalog Owner  Example Query: Determine whether the principal contractor@external.com can reach Account Admin privileges.

searchDocs.title: Analyze Impersonation Risk​
searchDocs.content: Discover lateral movement opportunities:  Users who can modify jobs that run as service principalsService principals with elevated privilegesClusters configured to run as specific service principals  Example Query: Identify principals that can run jobs as elevated service principals.

searchDocs.title: Detect Shares to All Account Users​
searchDocs.content: Find resources shared with the built-in account users group — which grants access to every user in the account:  dashboardsAI/BI Genie AgentsDatabricks Apps  Detection reads the audit log (system.access.audit) account-wide, so it captures shares across every running workspace without needing the permissions graph. Optional, opt-in remediation removes the offending ACL entry.  Example Query: List every dashboard, Genie Agent, and App shared with all account users in the last 30 days, and optionally revoke that access.

searchDocs.title: Detect Privileged Non-IdP Group Identities​
searchDocs.content: Surface privileged access that bypasses your identity provider's governance:  Groups that are not IdP-managed (no externalId) holding Account Admin or Workspace AdminUsers and service principals with those roles assigned directly  Detection uses the account SCIM API (account-wide) plus workspace admins group membership. Optional, opt-in remediation removes the account_admin role via SCIM.  Example Query: List every locally-managed group and every directly-assigned user that holds Account Admin.

searchDocs.title: Build an Account Denylist​
searchDocs.content: Help scale the account access denylist:  Inactive-user group candidates — account groups ranked by how many members have no recent system.access.audit activity (good groups to deny without disrupting active users)Entra ID dynamic-group rule builder — a guided builder that emits dynamic membership rule syntax (guest users, mail/UPN domain match, department, company, disabled accounts), combinable with AND/OR, so a single denylist entry can cover thousands of identities  Example Query: Which IdP groups have the most inactive members, and what Entra rule denies all guest users?

searchDocs.title: Generate Compliance Reports​
searchDocs.content: Produce audit-ready reports showing:  Over-privileged users (access to 50+ resources)Orphaned resources (created by departed users)High-risk principals (multiple escalation paths)Secret scope access patterns

searchDocs.title: Best Practices​
searchDocs.content: Regular Data Collection: Run the data collection job regularly (weekly or bi-weekly) to maintain an up-to-date permissions graph as your environment changes.Web UI for Ad-Hoc Queries: Use the web UI for ad-hoc queries and quick access audits. Use the notebooks for automated reporting and compliance checks.Point-in-Time Data: Permissions data represents a point-in-time snapshot. For critical access reviews, ensure data collection has run recently.

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: Developers sometimes hardcode credentials — API keys, tokens, passwords — directly in notebook source, workspace files, or cluster configurations and forget to remove them. These secrets can persist for months, readable by anyone with access to the code or cluster. SAT's secret scanning helps you find and remediate them.

searchDocs.title: What It Does​
searchDocs.content: SAT scans for hardcoded credentials with TruffleHog (800+ detector patterns) across three surfaces in one run:  Notebook source — every notebook in scope.Workspace files — .py, .sql, .json, .yaml, .sh, and other text/config files.Cluster configurations — spark_env_vars and the init scripts clusters reference (including init scripts on FUSE mount paths such as /Volumes/... and /dbfs/..., scanned as files so secrets in shell scripts are caught, not just env values).  Configure coverage and custom detection rules from the app (Credential Exposure → Scan Settings; see Usage).  Detection covers:  AWS credentials: Access keys, secret keys, session tokensAzure secrets: Service principal keys, storage account keysGCP credentials: Service account keys, API keysGitHub tokens: Personal access tokens, OAuth tokensAPI keys: Stripe, Slack, SendGrid, and other service API keysDatabase passwords: Connection strings with embedded credentialsPrivate keys: SSH keys, RSA keys, and other cryptographic materialDatabricks-specific tokens: DKEA, DAPI, DOSE tokens  Built for heavy workspaces Init scripts referenced via FUSE mount paths are scanned alongside spark_env_vars.TruffleHog is installed from a pinned tagged release for supply-chain reproducibility.The cluster scan de-duplicates the many job clusters a busy workspace produces (scanning one per distinct env-var set), retries Delta writes under concurrent load, and fails loudly rather than silently reporting an incomplete scan as clean.

searchDocs.title: Why It Matters​
searchDocs.content: Hardcoded credentials — in notebooks, workspace files, or cluster configurations — pose significant security risks:  Persistent Exposure: Secrets stay in the code/config until explicitly removedBroad Access: Anyone who can read the notebook, file, or cluster config can see themCompliance Violations: Hardcoded secrets violate security best practices and compliance requirementsAttack Surface: Exposed credentials can be used to access cloud resources, databases, and external services

searchDocs.title: How It Works​
searchDocs.content: Discovery: SAT enumerates notebooks and workspace files in scope, plus cluster configurationsPattern Detection: TruffleHog scans the content with 800+ detector patterns (plus any custom rules you add)Typing: Each finding is tagged with its object type — Notebook, File, or ClusterReporting: Findings appear on the app's Credential Exposure page and are stored in your SAT schema (notebooks_secret_scan_results for notebooks and files, clusters_secret_scan_results for clusters)

searchDocs.title: Credential Exposure page​
searchDocs.content: The app's Credential Exposure page shows all findings together — notebooks, files, and clusters — with per-workspace and per-detector rollups, a type filter, and a summary. Each finding's object name links straight to the notebook, file, or cluster in its workspace.

searchDocs.title: Database tables​
searchDocs.content: Results are stored in your SAT schema:  notebooks_secret_scan_results — notebook and workspace-file findings (object_type is notebook or file), with the object id/path/name, detector, the secret's SHA‑256 (never the value), workspace, and scan time.clusters_secret_scan_results — cluster findings, with the cluster id/name, the config field/key, detector, SHA‑256, workspace, and scan time.

searchDocs.title: Example Finding​
searchDocs.content: Object: /Repos/dev/etl/load_orders (Notebook) Detector: AWS Workspace: 1657683783405196 Recommendation: remove the hardcoded value; read it from a Unity Catalog secret

searchDocs.title: Remediation​
searchDocs.content: Remove hardcoded secrets Remove hardcoded credentials from source and configuration and store them asUnity Catalog secrets, then read them at runtime. UC secrets are governed by Unity Catalog, and dbutilsredacts their values in cell output and logs.

searchDocs.title: Recommended approach​
searchDocs.content: Store the secret in Unity Catalog — create it under a catalog.schema you govern (see the Unity Catalog secrets guide). UC secrets use the three-level namespace catalog.schema.secret.Remove the hardcoded value from the notebook, workspace file, or cluster spark_env_vars.Read it at runtime with dbutils.secrets.get.Grant access so the principals and compute that need it can read the secret.

searchDocs.title: Example: read a Unity Catalog secret instead of hardcoding​
searchDocs.content: Before (insecure):  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY"   After (secure) — read it from a Unity Catalog secret:  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = dbutils.secrets.get( catalog="main", schema="prod_app", key="aws_secret_access_key" )   dbutils.secrets.get requires serverless (environment version 4+) or classic compute on Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS or later.  Cluster environment variables A cluster's spark_env_vars can't reference a Unity Catalog secret directly — move the value into a UC secret and read it in code with dbutils.secrets.get.

searchDocs.title: Configuration​
searchDocs.content: Configure secret scanning from the app — Credential Exposure → Scan Settings & Custom Detection Rules. Changes save to the scanner's config and take effect on the next scan run, with no redeploy and no editing notebooks.  Scan coverage — scan all notebooks and files (the default, so the view reflects your complete current exposure) or only objects modified in the lastN days (a faster delta scan; the view then shows only that window).Scan cluster configurations — on by default; turn it off to scan notebook and workspace-file source only.Custom detection rules — add your own patterns (name, keywords, regex) on top of the built-in detectors, listed as editable rows you can change or delete. Rules apply to both notebook/file and cluster scans.  Clusters are always fully scanned The coverage window applies to notebook and file discovery. Cluster configurations are always scanned in full; to keep a busy workspace tractable, job clusters that share the same spark_env_vars are de-duplicated so only one per distinct set is fetched and scanned.

searchDocs.title: Which workspaces are scanned​
searchDocs.content: Secret scanning follows the same collection scope as the rest of SAT (Data Collection → Manage): This workspace only scans the current workspace; Multiple workspaces scans every workspace the SAT service principal is a workspace admin of. Maintain that set with Manage → Sync workspaces — add the service principal as a workspace admin on a workspace and sync to include it, remove it and sync to drop it. See theUsage guide for the full workflow.

searchDocs.title: Firewall Allowlist Requirements​
searchDocs.content: If your environment uses firewalls, you may need to allowlist the following GitHub domains to ensure secret scanning can download TruffleHog and access required resources:  Firewall Configuration If you encounter connection issues during secret scanning, ensure your firewall allows outbound connections to the following domains:  Allow outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to all of these — the binary download redirects across several of them, so an incomplete list still fails:  raw.githubusercontent.com — the install scriptgithub.com — the release download URL (returns a redirect)release-assets.githubusercontent.com — where that redirect points (the TruffleHog binary); current GitHub release-asset hostobjects.githubusercontent.com — legacy GitHub release-asset host (older releases / fallback)  api.github.com is not required — the TruffleHog version is pinned, so the installer builds the download URL directly rather than querying the API.  The binary is cached per compute container and re-downloaded whenever the scan lands on a fresh (cold) serverless container, so this egress must stay open, not just during the first run. If opening egress to GitHub isn't acceptable, host the pinned TruffleHog release on an internal mirror instead.

searchDocs.title: Best Practices​
searchDocs.content: Regular Scanning Run secret scans regularly (weekly or bi-weekly) to catch newly introduced secrets before they become security risks.  Automated Workflows Use the app's alerts to notify your security team when new secrets are detected in notebooks, files, or cluster configurations.  Developer Training Educate developers on using Unity Catalog secrets instead of hardcoding credentials. Include this in onboarding and security training.  False Positives Some patterns may trigger false positives (e.g. a cloud-resource identifier that looks token-shaped, or a template that wraps a value read from a secret). Review findings carefully, and exclude a detector or tune custom rules from the app's scan settings if needed.

searchDocs.title: Learn More​
searchDocs.content: Usage Guide - Set up, run collection, and view resultsPermissions Analysis - Understand who can access cluster configurationsThe SAT App - How the app is organized

searchDocs.title: Step 1 — Complete first-run setup​
searchDocs.content: The first time you open the app it shows a setup screen. Provide:  Catalog & schema — where SAT stores its results. The app creates the schema and owns it. Pick a catalog you can access, or type any catalog name.SQL warehouse — runs the analysis queries and alerts.Account credentials (optional, for account-wide data) — an Account IDand a service principal's client ID + secret (that SP must hold theAccount admin role). These unlock Account/Workspace/Metastore Admin detection, account users & groups, and other account-wide reports. They are stored as Unity Catalog secrets — no secret scope required. Without them, SAT reports on the current workspace only.Collection scope & compute — Workspaces to scan: this workspace only, or multiple workspaces. This governs both resource-permission collection and secret scanning: this workspace only restricts both to the current workspace; multiple workspacescovers every workspace the service principal administers. To add a workspace to the multi-workspace set, make the service principal a workspace admin there, then run Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces (see below). Identity and admin data is always account-wide when account credentials are set.Job compute: serverless (recommended) or classic. Classic is offered when the workspace supports it; a genuinely serverless-only workspace shows classic as unavailable.Scan notebook & folder permissions: off by default; turning it on walks the whole workspace tree so each collection run takes longer to complete.  Everything is reconfigurable You can change any of these later from Settings (catalog/schema, warehouse, model, credentials) and Data Collection → Manage (scope, compute, notebook/folder collection). The collection jobs are re-provisioned automatically when you change compute or scope.  Adding or removing workspaces — Sync workspaces Which workspaces SAT scans is driven by whether its service principal is aworkspace admin of each one. After adding (or removing) the service principal as a workspace admin, open Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces: SAT lists the account's workspaces and enables the ones the service principal administers. It's an explicit, in-app action — no manual SQL and no re-running a collection job. Scope and sync work together: switching collection scope to "Multiple workspaces" runs a sync for you, so the common first-time path is just picking Multiple. The standalone Sync workspaces button is for refreshing the set afterwards when you add or remove the service principal as an admin. If you Sync while scope is still "This workspace only," the extra workspaces are enabled but not scanned until you switch to Multiple — the app tells you so.

searchDocs.title: Step 2 — Run data collection​
searchDocs.content: On the Data Collection page you'll see SAT's collection jobs (initializer, permissions data collection, account reports, and the secret scanner). They run on a schedule, and you can trigger any of them on demand.  Collection can take several minutes per workspace, depending on account size.  The app owns the jobs SAT creates and manages these jobs itself under the app's service principal. You don't import or schedule any notebooks — adjust the schedule, scope, and compute from the app.

searchDocs.title: Step 3 — View results​
searchDocs.content: All results are in the app:  Principal Analysis / Resource Analysis — who can access what, with escalation and impersonation risk. See Permissions Analysis.Credential Exposure — hardcoded secrets in notebooks and cluster configs. See Secret Scanning.  Because the app queries as the signed-in user, Unity Catalog enforces each viewer's own grants — people see only the results they are entitled to.

searchDocs.title: Step 4 — Configure secret scanning (optional)​
searchDocs.content: On the Credential Exposure page, open Scan Settings & Custom Detection Rules to:  Scan coverage — scan all notebooks (recommended, so the view reflects your complete current exposure) or only notebooks modified in the last N days.Custom detection rules — add your own patterns (name, keywords, regex) on top of SAT's built-in detectors. Rules are listed as editable rows you can change or delete.  Changes are saved to the scanner's config and take effect on the next scan run — no redeploy and no editing notebooks. More detail on theSecret Scanning page.

searchDocs.title: Step 5 — Set up alerts (optional)​
searchDocs.content: On the Alerts page, create email/notification alerts on secret-scan findings (for example, "any hardcoded credential detected"). Pick the condition, how often to check, and who to notify. Alerts are standard Databricks SQL alerts, so they also appear under Alerts in the workspace and keep working if the app is ever removed.  Admins only Creating, editing, and deleting alerts is restricted to workspace or account admins. Other users can view alerts and run the read-only "test condition" check, but the create/edit/delete controls are hidden for them.

searchDocs.title: Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Note SAT is especially beneficial to customers on Databricks Premium or Enterprise tiers, where Unity Catalog and the richer access controls SAT analyzes are available.  Before proceeding with the installation, make sure you have the following prerequisites:  Python 3.9 or higher (to run the installer locally)Databricks CLI installed with a logged-in profile (See here.)A Databricks SQL warehouse (the app uses it to run analysis queries and alerts; the installer can create one)(Optional, for account-wide data) a Databricks Account ID and a service principal with the Account admin role — you enter these in the app's setup, not at install timePyPI access on the machine running the installer (to install the installer's Python dependencies)  SAT can be set up on any of the cloud platforms where Databricks is hosted. Please follow the setup guide specific to your cloud provider:  AWS Setup GuideAzure Setup GuideGCP Setup Guide  Terraform Install SAT can be deployed using Terraform. If your organization uses Terraform, it is recommended to follow the Terraform-based deployment instructions: SAT AWS Terraform deploymentSAT Azure Terraform deploymentSAT GCP Terraform deployment  Manual install (no CLI / install.sh / Terraform) Prefer not to use install.sh, Terraform, or the Databricks CLI? You can deploy the app from the Databricks UI: Get the code into the workspace — add the SAT repo as a Git folder (Repos → Add repo, paste the GitHub URL), or download the repo ZIP from GitHub and upload the app/security-analysis-tool/ folder to a workspace folder.Create the app — Compute → Apps → Create app, name it security-analysis, and point its source at the app/security-analysis-tool folder from step 1. That folder already contains everything the app needs, including the bundled collection notebooks and SAT SDK (in assets_data.py and lib/).Add the app's resources — in the app's Edit screen, bind a SQL warehouse resource (CAN USE), and under User authorization add the sql and genie scopes. (install.sh and Terraform set these automatically; a manual install sets them here.)Deploy the app, then Open it and complete the in-app setup (catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, and optionally account credentials). The app provisions its own collection jobs from there — no notebooks to import by hand. The automated paths (install.sh, Terraform) do exactly these steps for you; this is the same result done manually.

searchDocs.title: Uninstalling SAT​
searchDocs.content: Note SAT stores its results in the Unity Catalog schema you chose during setup. To remove them, drop that schema (replace with your catalog/schema): drop schema `<catalog>`.`<schema>` cascade;

searchDocs.title: Standard Setup​
searchDocs.content: Delete the security-analysis app (Compute → Apps).Delete the SAT-provisioned collection jobs (they are tagged Application: SAT — e.g. SAT Initializer, SAT Permissions Analysis - Data Collection, the account-report jobs, and SAT Secrets Scanner).Delete the /Workspace/Applications/SAT folder.

searchDocs.title: Terraform Setup​
searchDocs.content: Run the terraform destroy command (then remove any jobs the app provisioned, as above).

searchDocs.title: Step 1: Create Service Principal​
searchDocs.content: The service principal lets SAT authenticate to the Databricks account and workspace APIs to collect security information.  Databricks OAuth — no Microsoft Entra / tenant needed SAT authenticates with Databricks OAuth, the same way it does on AWS and GCP. It reads only the Databricks account and workspace APIs, so there is no Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) token, no tenant ID, and no Azure subscription involved. You give the service principal a Databricks OAuth secret (not an Azure AD app client secret).  How to create a Service Principal Follow these steps in the Databricks Account Console: Navigate to the Databricks Account ConsoleClick on User management in the left sidebarSelect Service principals → Add service principalChoose Databricks managed, enter a name (e.g., "SAT-Service-Principal"), and click Add If you prefer to use an existing Microsoft Entra ID application, choose Microsoft Entra ID managed instead and paste its Application (client) ID. Either kind works — SAT only needs the Databricks OAuth secret created in Step 2. Grant the Account Admin roleAssign the Workspace Admin role for each workspace to be monitoredAdd to the Metastore Admin group or roleAdd the Service Principal to each workspace you want to analyze Required Permissions: Account Admin roleWorkspace Admin role for each workspaceMetastore admin group membership

searchDocs.title: Step 2: Create a Databricks OAuth Secret​
searchDocs.content: How to create the OAuth secret In the Databricks Account Console: Open the service principal you created in Step 1Go to the Secrets section → under OAuth secrets, click Generate secretCopy and save the Secret and the Client ID immediately (the secret is shown only once) This is a Databricks OAuth secret, used with the standard client_id / client_secret OAuth flow — the same model as AWS and GCP. You do not create an Azure AD "Certificates & secrets" client secret. 📚 Learn more about Databricks OAuth (M2M) for service principals

searchDocs.title: Step 3: Run Installation​
searchDocs.content: Credentials Required Have these ready for the app's in-app setup (you enter them in the app after install, not during install.sh): 🔑 Databricks Account ID🔑 Service Principal Client ID (from Step 1)🔑 Databricks OAuth Secret (from Step 2) No Azure tenant ID or subscription ID is needed.

searchDocs.title: Installation Steps​
searchDocs.content: Run these commands on your workstation or a VM with internet access and Databricks workspace connectivity:  1. Clone the SAT repository:  git clone https://github.com/databricks-industry-solutions/security-analysis-tool.git cd security-analysis-tool   Databricks CLI Required Make sure the target workspace has a profile configured in the Databricks CLI.  2. Make the installation script executable and run it:  chmod +x install.sh ./install.sh   Proxy Support Proxies are supported! You can add your HTTP and HTTPS proxy values during the install.sh script when prompted.  3. Follow the interactive prompts:  The installation script will guide you through the setup process. Here's what it looks like:      Finish setup in the app After install.sh deploys the app, open it (Compute → Apps → security-analysis) and complete the in-app setup — results catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, and (optionally) account credentials for account-wide data. Permissions Analysis is built into the app; there is no separate app to configure.  Deploying the app — choose the source folder install.sh uploads the app code to /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool and deploys it for you. If you ever deploy or redeploy from the Databricks Apps UI (Compute → Apps → security-analysis → Deploy), you must select that folder as the app's source code path. From the CLI the equivalent is databricks apps deploy security-analysis --source-code-path /Workspace/Applications/SAT/files/app/security-analysis-tool.  Scanning multiple workspaces To cover more than the workspace SAT is installed in, add the SAT service principal as a workspace admin on each workspace you want scanned, then in the app open Data Collection → Manage, set Compute & scope to Multiple workspaces (switching to Multiple runs a workspace sync for you), and confirm the panel's "Will scan: N workspaces" count. Use Manage → Sync workspaces any time you later add or remove the service principal as an admin. See the usage guide for the full workflow.  Congratulations! 🎉 You've successfully installed SAT on Azure Databricks.  Installation Complete SAT is now ready to analyze your Databricks workspaces. Click here for a detailed guide on how to run and use it.

searchDocs.content: Navigate to the relevant cloud directory:  cd security-analysis-tool/terraform/<cloud>/

searchDocs.title: Step 4: Configure Variables​
searchDocs.content: Create a terraform.tfvars file using the template.tfvars file as a base.Refer to the variables.tf for descriptions of the variables.Set all required variables for your deployment.  Azure-Specific Configuration​  Follow the Azure Setup Guide for variable setup.  Service Principal Role Requirements:​  Accounts Admin roleAdmin role for each workspaceMember of the metastore admin group  Refer to the documentation for workspace_url, workspace_id, and account_console_id

searchDocs.title: Step 5: Configure Azure CLI Credentials​
searchDocs.content: Set up Azure CLI credentials for the provider block in provider.tf.Use the Azure CLI to log in. The CLI will open a web browser for authentication:  az login   Proxies are now supported as part of SAT. You can add your HTTP and HTTPS links to use your proxies.  { "http": "http://example.com", "https": "https://example.com" }

searchDocs.title: Step 6: Run Terraform Commands​
searchDocs.content: Initialize Terraform:  terraform init   Plan Terraform Changes - create a plan to preview changes to your infrastructure:  terraform plan   Apply Terraform Plan - Execute the proposed changes:  terraform apply

searchDocs.title: Step 7: Open the SAT app and complete setup​
searchDocs.content: In the workspace, go to Compute → Apps → security-analysis and click Open.Complete the in-app setup — results catalog/schema, SQL warehouse, and (optionally) an Account ID + service-principal credentials for account-wide data, plus scan scope and compute. See the Usage Guide.The app provisions and schedules its own collection jobs; run them on demand from the Data Collection page. Results appear in the app — there is no separate dashboard to publish.

searchDocs.title: Supplemental Documentation​
searchDocs.content: Databricks Documentation TerraformDatabricks Terraform Provider Docs  Account credentials SAT no longer uses a sat_scope secret scope. Account credentials (for account-wide data) are entered in the app's setup flow and stored as Unity Catalog secrets. Permissions Analysis is built into the app — no separate app to configure.  Congratulations! 🎉 You are now ready to start using the SAT. Please click here for a detailed description on how to run and use it.

searchDocs.title: Checking your setup​
searchDocs.content: Built-in requirements check Instead of standalone diagnosis notebooks, the app has a built-in requirements check. Open Settings → Re-run setup (or the first-run setup screen) and review the requirements checklist — it verifies, live, the account connection and the service principal's Account admin role, and flags configuration gaps so you can fix them before running collection. For a failed collection, open theData Collection page and inspect the job's last run.

searchDocs.title: Common Issues​
searchDocs.content: Account-wide data is missing or credentials failed Symptom: Account/Workspace/Metastore Admin detection, account users & groups, and other account-wide reports are empty, or the setup screen reports the credentials didn't verify. Resolution: Account credentials are stored as Unity Catalog secrets (SAT no longer uses a sat_scope secret scope). In the app, open Settings → Account credentials (or re-run setup) and confirm: the Account ID is correct, andthe service principal's client ID + secret are valid and that SP holds the Account admin role. Credentials are verified before they're stored, so a failed save points to one of the above. After updating them, run data collection again from the Data Collection page.  Account authentication failed / the OAuth secret expired or was revoked Symptom: account-wide reports stop updating, or a collection run fails authenticating to the account API — the service principal's OAuth secret has most likely expired or been revoked. Resolution: In the account console, create a new OAuth secret for the service principal.In SAT, open Settings → Account credentials, paste the client ID and the new secret, and click Update credentials (verified before being stored as Unity Catalog secrets).Run data collection again. The jobs read the secret at run time, so the next run uses the new value — no redeploy or re-provision needed.Revoke the old secret in the account console. The setup requirements check (Settings → Re-run setup) verifies the account connection and the Account admin role live, so re-run it to confirm the fix is green.  A workspace isn't being scanned (or was skipped) Symptom: A workspace you expect to see has no findings, or a scan run reports it as skipped. Resolution: SAT scans a workspace only when both are true: The service principal is a workspace admin there, and the workspace is enabled. Scan coverage is keyed on the SP being a workspace admin of each workspace. Add the SP as a workspace admin on the target, then run Data Collection → Manage → Sync workspaces — Sync lists the account's workspaces and sets analysis_enabled on the ones the SP administers (account_workspaces table). Removing the SP as admin and syncing again drops the workspace.Collection scope is Multiple workspaces. With scope set to This workspace only, both resource collection and secret scanning stay on the current workspace regardless of what's enabled. Set scope to Multiple workspaces in Data Collection → Manage. On serverless compute, reaching a remote workspace also requires the account to be enrolled in serverless cross-workspace access (a preview — ask your account team). Workspaces that still can't be reached are skipped and recorded, not failed. Classic compute can reach any workspace the SP administers.  Firewall Blocking Databricks Accounts Console - Connection Reset Error Error: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/databricks/python/lib/python3.8/site-packages/urllib3/connectionpool.py", line 670, in urlopen httplib_response = self._make_request( File "/databricks/python/lib/python3.8/site-packages/urllib3/connectionpool.py", line 381, in _make_request self._validate_conn(conn) File "/databricks/python/lib/python3.8/site-packages/urllib3/connectionpool.py", line 978, in _validate_conn conn.connect() File "/databricks/python/lib/python3.8/site-packages/urllib3/connection.py", line 362, in connect self.sock = ssl_wrap_socket( File "/databricks/python/lib/python3.8/site-packages/urllib3/util/ssl_.py", line 386, in ssl_wrap_socket return context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=server_hostname) File "/usr/lib/python3.8/ssl.py", line 500, in wrap_socket return self.sslsocket_class._create( File "/usr/lib/python3.8/ssl.py", line 1040, in _create self.do_handshake() File "/usr/lib/python3.8/ssl.py", line 1309, in do_handshake self._sslobj.do_handshake() ConnectionResetError: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: Resolution: Run the following command in your notebook to test connectivity: %sh curl -X GET -H "Authorization: Basic /<base64 of userid:password/>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com/api/2.0/accounts/<account_id>/workspaces or %sh curl -u 'user:password' -X GET "Content-Type: application/json" https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com/api/2.0/accounts/<account_id>/workspaces If you don't see a JSON with a clean listing of workspaces, you are likely having a firewall issue that is blocking calls to the accounts console. Please have your infrastructure team add accounts.cloud.databricks.com to the allow-list. Ensure that the private IPv4 address from the NAT gateway is added to the IP allow list.  Permissions Analysis app shows 'missing sql scope' banner after an upgrade The Permissions Analysis app uses on-behalf-of-user (OBO) authentication. The required sql scope is declared in the SAT install templates, but each user must consent to the scope on first open after the upgrade. If you opened the app before upgrading, your browser session has a cached consent grant without sql and you'll see the banner. Resolution (try in order): Open the app URL in a private/incognito window — this triggers a fresh consent prompt.Or clear cookies for the workspace domain in your regular browser, then reopen the app.Or revoke the prior authorization from your account profile (if your workspace exposes a "Linked apps" list), then reopen. The full background and permanent setup is on the Permissions Analysis page.  Permissions Analysis app shows 'You don't have permission to read the SAT permissions analysis schema' The app runs Statement Execution as the calling user, so Unity Catalog enforces the user's grants on the Permissions Analysis tables. If the user does not have SELECT on those tables, the app renders a friendly banner instead of a SQL error. Resolution: an admin grants SELECT on the three tables to the user or group that needs to use the app. Replace <catalog> and <schema> with the values used during your SAT install: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_vertices TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_edges TO `<admin_group>`; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE `<catalog>`.`<schema>`.brickhound_collection_metadata TO `<admin_group>`;   Restricted egress / no PyPI access The SAT SDK wheel ships inside the app (under lib/) and is installed with--no-deps, so no PyPI access is needed for the SDK itself. Two things still reach out, and only matter for the features that use them: Secret scanning downloads the TruffleHog binary from GitHub. In a restricted-egress environment, allow-list raw.githubusercontent.com,github.com, release-assets.githubusercontent.com andobjects.githubusercontent.com (all HTTPS/443 — the download redirects across them, so an incomplete list still fails; see the Secret Scanningfirewall list) or provide an internal mirror.Classic compute pip-installs requests and PyYAML from PyPI for the scanners (serverless already has them). On classic compute without PyPI access, make those available from an internal package index.

searchDocs.title: Upgrading an existing app install​
searchDocs.content: Get the latest code (git pull on your checkout, or re-download the release).Redeploy with your usual path: Standard install: rerun ./install.sh.Terraform: terraform apply against the updated module.DABS bundle (advanced): databricks bundle deploy from the repo root. In the app, open Data Collection → Manage → Redeploy jobs so the collection jobs use the new bundled notebooks.  Your settings and data survive Configuration lives in the app's config file and credentials in Unity Catalog secrets; collected results live in your results schema. Redeploying the app or jobs does not clear them. "Redeploy jobs" updates the job definitions/notebooks; "Re-run initializer" rebuilds the result tables' schema without dropping prior runs.  Network-policy / egress changes If a redeploy changes the app's network policy or egress, stop and start the app (not just redeploy) so the new network settings take effect.

searchDocs.title: Moving from a pre-1.0 (classic) install​
searchDocs.content: Versions before 1.0 ran SAT as a set of notebooks (Initializer + Driver) with standalone dashboards and core security posture checks. 1.0 replaces them with the single SAT app, focused on access/permissions risk and exposed secrets. The core security posture checks are now native in theDatabricks Governance Hub Security tab. After deploying 1.0:  Use the app for everything — permissions, secrets, and alerts. The oldGeneral and Executive dashboards and the core security posture checks are retired (the checks live in the Governance Hub now).If Governance Hub isn't available in your environment (e.g. AWS GovCloud) and you still need the core security posture checks, use SAT v0.9.1.Complete the app's first-run setup (catalog/schema, warehouse, and optionally account credentials). You can point it at your existing results schema.Retire the old SAT Initializer Notebook / SAT Driver Notebook workflows — the app provisions and schedules its own collection jobs.  Re-consent for per-user authorization The app queries as the signed-in user (on-behalf-of) so Unity Catalog enforces each viewer's grants. Users who opened an earlier app build before user authorization was configured re-consent once — seePermissions Analysis → Re-consent after an upgradeand Troubleshooting.
